paper_did: Synthesized an equiatomic CrMoNbWV high‐entropy alloy (HEA) from elemental powders via mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at three different temperatures (1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C).

Characterized the alloy’s microstructure using XRD and SEM/EDS, showing a primary BCC solid solution with partial decomposition into Laves phases (Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb) and oxide phases (NbVO4–VO), with evident grain coarsening and carburization effects from the graphite die during SPS.
Tested mechanical properties (compressive strength, hardness), wear behavior (using ASTM G65 abrasion tests) and corrosion resistance (electrochemical tests in 0.5 M H2SO4 at room temperature).
paper_reported: The MA powders yielded a BCC structure that, after SPS, partially decomposed into Laves phases and oxide precipitates; the volume fraction of the brittle Laves phases decreased with increasing sintering temperature while oxide morphology changed (with coarser oxides at higher temperature).

The sintered HEA exhibited high compressive strength (2700–2870 MPa) and good wear and corrosion resistance, although low plasticity was observed due to the intergranular localization of brittle phases.
Carburization during SPS (via carbon diffusion from the graphite die) resulted in interstitial carbon incorporation and carbide formation in the surface layer, which modified local wear properties.
paper_proposed: Future work will focus on using iron‐free powders, investigating the effect of SPS duration, and applying additional post‐process heat treatments to further refine the alloy’s structure and properties.

The observed microstructural evolution (e.g., reduction of Laves phase content with higher SPS temperature and coarsening of oxide inclusions) is linked to the corresponding changes in mechanical and corrosion properties.

paper_did: Synthesized AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy via arc melting, suction-casting, and subsequent thermo‐mechanical processing.
Employed a novel hybrid‐rolling process combining cryo‐rolling (ε ≈ 1.2) and warm‐rolling at 600 °C (ε ≈ 1.2) to achieve a total strain of ~2.4 (90% thickness reduction).

Characterized the microstructure using EBSD, TEM, HAADF-STEM, and nano-beam diffraction, revealing retained lamellar regions (ordered L12 and B2 phases) alongside transformed nanocrystalline regions with compositional variations.
Performed tensile tests that established an outstanding mechanical performance with yield strength (σYS ~1900 MPa), ultimate tensile strength (σUTS ~2000 MPa), and uniform elongation (~8%).
paper_reported: The hybrid-rolled alloy exhibits an unprecedented combination of high strength and acceptable ductility in bulk form.

A dual structural-compositional heterogeneous microstructure is formed, wherein retained lamellar regions and adjacent nanocrystalline regions contain distinct ordered/disordered phases with varying chemical compositions.

The outstanding mechanical properties are primarily attributed to mechanisms such as nanostructuring and the generation of long-range back stress from the high density of interfaces and strain gradients.
paper_proposed: Future work will focus on quantifying the back stress and further tuning the microstructural heterogeneities to enhance the mechanical performance.
The novel hybrid processing route is proposed for exploitation in tailoring the nanostructure and properties of other multiphase/dual-phase high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase Boundary Oxide Disruption Accelerates Degradation due to Selective Passive Film Breakdown at Heterogeneous Interfaces.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting heterogeneous phase distribution with inherent phase boundaries that form distinct passive films under ambient conditions.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the alloy chemistry by minor reactive microalloying (e.g., trace boron addition) that preferentially segregates at phase boundaries to improve the adhesion and stability of the passive oxide film.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (e.g., above 300°C) where oxidation kinetics are enhanced and mechanical abrasion is significant.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The chemical composition and integrity of the passive oxide film at phase boundaries between the eutectic phases.
hypotheses.mechanism: At elevated temperature, wear mechanically removes sections of the incipient passive oxide film. The heterogeneous chemical and structural nature of the eutectic phases causes the passive film to form unevenly. Without stabilization, once removed, the exposed phase boundaries undergo rapid oxidation and localized corrosion. Boron segregation can tie together the interface, promoting a more continuous and adherent passive layer, thereby reducing film breakdown and subsequent galvanic corrosion. This interplay of micro-scale film disruption and local galvanic effects leads to accelerated overall degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy without boron, the boron-doped alloy should exhibit a lower total degradation rate. Individually, the wear rate and corrosion current density should decrease due to improved passive film stability at the vulnerable phase boundaries. Expected improvements are moderate (~20–30% reduction in degradation metrics), though precise values are uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Multi-phase eutectic HEA without microalloying additives, showing localized film breakdown at phase boundaries under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: Effective only during high-temperature operation (above ambient, e.g., >300°C) and under simultaneous mechanical wear conditions; the beneficial effect of boron may vanish under low-temperature or static conditions.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact degree of improvement in passive film stability and the quantitative reduction in degradation rates remain to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic HEA samples: one with trace boron addition (e.g., ≤0.5 at.%) and one without. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature (e.g., 350°C) simultaneous wear–corrosion conditions in a corrosive environment. Characterize passive film integrity via surface microscopy and measure degradation rates via wear tracks and electrochemical tests.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion parameters (icorr, Rct)
Wear rate (e.g., via Archard’s law)
Passive film morphological integrity at phase boundaries (SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (i.e., reduction in both wear and corrosion metrics and improved film integrity) relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that boron addition in HEA coatings improves passive film stability and wear resistance by affecting microstructural features (PMC12565319).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the concept to eutectic high-entropy alloys at high temperatures, proposing that localized passive film disruption at phase boundaries is the dominant degradation pathway under coupled wear–corrosion, and that trace boron can mitigate this by stabilizing interfacial films.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Coarse Eutectic Spacing Amplifies Degradation via Enhanced Interface Exposure and Localized Oxidation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with relatively coarse interlamellar or discontinuous eutectic structures, featuring large phase boundaries that serve as sites for passive film formation.
hypotheses.intervention: Process modification to refine the eutectic spacing—achieved by increasing the cooling rate during solidification or by adding microalloying elements (other than boron) known to promote nucleation—thereby reducing the size of the individual eutectic colonies.
hypotheses.conditions: Operational conditions combine elevated temperature (to speed up oxidation kinetics) with mechanical wear in corrosive environments.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The size and distribution of the eutectic phases and their interphase boundaries that control the area and continuity of the passive oxide film.
hypotheses.mechanism: Coarse eutectic spacing results in extensive, contiguous phase boundaries where passive oxide films are formed. Under wear, these large interfacial areas are more susceptible to mechanical rupture and localized removal of the film, leading to accelerated corrosion at the interfaces. Refining the eutectic spacing reduces the effective phase boundary area susceptible to film breakdown. A more homogenous and fine-scale microstructure distributes stresses more evenly during wear, thereby diminishing localized damage and slowing corrosion initiation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy with coarse eutectic structures, the refined microstructure should show a reduction in both overall degradation and in separate wear and corrosion metrics. The anticipated outcome is a moderated decrease in total degradation (e.g., wear rate and corrosion current density) though the precise magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: The same multi-phase eutectic HEA produced via conventional cooling rates leading to coarse eutectic spacing, which exhibits accelerated degradation due to extensive interface exposure.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant under conditions where the cooling rate during processing can be reliably controlled and where the operating temperature is high enough to activate oxidation processes.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative reductions in degradation rates are subject to experimental verification and may depend on the specific alloy composition and processing limits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one processed with a high cooling rate (refined eutectic spacing) and one with standard cooling (coarse spacing). Subject them to identical high-temperature wear–corrosion tests. Analyze microstructural features, measure wear rates, and perform electrochemical corrosion tests.
measurements: Eutectic spacing characterization (optical/SEM imaging)
Wear rate and friction coefficient
Electrochemical corrosion parameters (icorr, passivation behavior)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined microstructure samples do not exhibit a statistically lower degradation rate and improved localized corrosion resistance compared to the coarse samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the principle that finer microstructural features (such as refined grains or eutectic spacing) lead to improved mechanical and corrosive performance (PMC12565319, TXT::wikipedia::Eutectic_system::008).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis shifts focus from chemical modification to controlling microstructural scale (eutectic spacing) as the key parameter dictating the susceptibility to coupled wear–corrosion degradation at high temperatures.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Thermally Induced Residual Stress Cracking at Phase Interfaces Drives Accelerated Degradation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy containing phases with mismatched thermal expansion coefficients, generating inherent residual stresses at phase interfaces during processing.
hypotheses.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition to better match the thermal expansion coefficients of the constituent phases (for instance by partially substituting one element with another of similar size or modulating the content of a specific element) so as to reduce the residual stresses that develop during thermal cycling.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposure to elevated temperatures with thermal cycling and simultaneous wear and corrosion, which exacerbate the development of residual stresses and induce microcracking at phase interfaces.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The density and distribution of microcracks at phase interfaces induced by thermal expansion mismatch and exacerbated by mechanical wear.
hypotheses.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the different phases within the eutectic HEA expand at different rates due to mismatched thermal expansion coefficients. The resulting residual stresses concentrate at the interfaces leading to the formation of microcracks. These microcracks serve as preferential sites for both mechanical wear penetration and accelerated corrosion due to increased exposure of fresh, unoxidized material. This coupled mechanism of residual stress-induced cracking and subsequent degradation accelerates overall material loss.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: When compared to a baseline alloy with higher mismatch (and thus higher crack density), the modified alloy with reduced thermal expansion mismatch should display fewer interfacial cracks, resulting in lower wear rates and lower corrosion current densities. The overall degradation should be measurably reduced, though the exact percentage reduction is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: The existing multi-phase eutectic HEA in its standard composition, which exhibits inherent thermal expansion mismatch and associated interfacial cracking under cyclic high-temperature wear–corrosion conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is most relevant under conditions involving significant thermal cycling and high service temperatures; its impact may be diminished in isothermal conditions.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the formation of residual stresses and microcracks is well-understood, the quantification of their contribution to overall degradation in these alloys under service conditions remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two versions of the alloy: one with the standard composition and one with modified composition to minimize thermal expansion mismatch. Expose both to controlled cycles of elevated temperature (with thermal cycling) combined with wear and corrosion tests. Evaluate the density of microcracks (via microscopic imaging) and perform wear and electrochemical corrosion measurements.
measurements: Quantification of interfacial microcrack density (SEM analysis)
Wear rate measurements
Electrochemical corrosion parameters (icorr, Rct)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in microcrack density and associated wear/corrosion degradation relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the known influence of thermal expansion mismatch on residual stress formation and its subsequent effect on corrosion and wear (corroborated by high-temperature corrosion principles in TXT::wikipedia::High-temperature corrosion::014).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis integrates thermal cycling-induced residual stress effects with mechanical wear, proposing that interfacial microcracking is the primary driver of accelerated coupled degradation in eutectic HEAs, and that alloy composition modification to reduce mismatch can mitigate this effect.

paper_did: Fabricated AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (with x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding with high-purity gas‐atomized elemental powders.
Varied the boron content to induce in situ formation of TiB2 and to modify the microstructure (dendritic and interdendritic regions) without altering the primary BCC and σ phases.
Characterized the coatings using XRD, SEM, and EDS to determine phase composition, morphology, and elemental distribution.

Measured microhardness, performed room‐temperature wear tests (analyzing friction coefficients, wear rates, and worn surface morphology), and assessed corrosion resistance via electrochemical tests (potentiodynamic polarization and EIS) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
paper_reported: B addition preserves the base BCC and σ phases while promoting the formation of in situ TiB2, which refines the BCC phase and alters the phase size and morphology with increasing B content.

Microhardness increases with B content and the optimum wear resistance is achieved at x = 1; however, excessive boron (x = 1.5) leads to agglomerated TiB2 particles that spall under wear, undermining performance.

Corrosion resistance improves with a small amount of boron (x = 0.5) due to a more stable passive film, but excessive boron degrades film integrity due to the defects introduced by large TiB2 clusters.
The study links microstructural features (e.g., grain refinement, TiB2 particle distribution) to performance improvements and provides a basis for further optimization.
paper_proposed: Further optimization of the coating’s performance through compositional tuning and post‐processing to address specific service environments, machinability, and long‐term stability.
Expansion of the generalized design strategy for high-performance HEA coatings to enable reliable service across a broad range of applications.

hypotheses.hypothesis: TiB2 Agglomeration‐Induced Passive Film Disruption Accelerates Coupled Degradation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA produced by laser cladding in which in situ formed TiB2 particles exist in a range of morphologies from well‐dispersed fine particles to locally agglomerated/coarse clusters.
hypotheses.intervention: Control and intentionally modify processing parameters (e.g., slight increases in boron content or adjustment of laser parameters) that promote TiB2 agglomeration, thereby altering their dispersion within the dendritic (DR) region.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (e.g., >300°C) where oxidation kinetics and mechanical abrasion are both activated.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The morphology and spatial distribution of TiB2 reinforcements and the resulting continuity or disruption of the passive oxide film along phase boundaries.
hypotheses.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the TiB2 coarse agglomerates create local stress concentrations and surface irregularities that disrupt the formation and adherence of the protective oxide film. When wear processes mechanically remove portions of an already heterogeneous oxide layer, these agglomerated regions become preferential sites for localized oxidation and enhanced galvanic attack. The mismatch between the bulky TiB2 clusters and the softer matrix exacerbates stress intensity during sliding, further promoting film spallation and accelerating overall degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy with a well‐dispersed, fine TiB2 distribution, the alloy engineered to have more agglomerated/coarse TiB2 is expected to exhibit higher wear rates and increased corrosion current densities—resulting in a higher total degradation rate. Improvement or degradation is measurable in both wear track damage (increased wear depth and width) and electrochemical corrosion parameters (higher icorr and lower passive film resistance), with an anticipated effect on the order of a moderate increase (>20–30% more degradation) subject to experimental quantification.
hypotheses.baseline: The same multi-phase eutectic HEA with fine, uniformly dispersed TiB2 particles which form a relatively continuous passive film under similar elevated temperature wear–corrosion conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is significant only when the operating temperature sufficiently accelerates oxidation kinetics and the wear conditions mechanically stress the heterogeneous oxide film; under milder conditions the effect may be negligible.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of TiB2 agglomeration on degradation rates requires investigation, and the trade-off between particle size and beneficial reinforcement (at lower temperatures) versus detrimental effects (at elevated temperatures) remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic HEA samples via laser cladding that differ primarily in the distribution of TiB2: one with a controlled fine dispersion and one with intentionally agglomerated/coarse TiB2 (achieved via slight processing changes or higher boron levels). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature wear–corrosion tests (e.g., 350°C in a corrosive medium under steady sliding wear).
measurements: Characterization of TiB2 size distribution and dispersion via SEM/EDS.
Wear rate and damage assessment (wear track profiling).
Electrochemical corrosion tests (icorr, Rct, EIS measurements) with mapping of passive film integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with agglomerated TiB2 do not show statistically significant higher wear rates, lower passive film resistance, and increased corrosion current density than the finely dispersed control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s findings on the role of in situ formed TiB2 particles influencing wear and corrosion, extending the concept by linking TiB2 morphology (coarse agglomeration) at elevated temperature to passive film disruption under coupled degradation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes that not only the presence but the size and distribution of TiB2 particles are critical at elevated temperatures; coarse TiB2 agglomerates act as focal points for passive film failure, a mechanistic detail not addressed in the original work.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Differential Oxide Growth at Dendritic–Interdendritic Interfaces Accelerates Degradation via Enhanced Galvanic Coupling.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA with distinct dendritic (DR) and interdendritic (IR) regions that naturally form different passive oxide layers due to compositional variations.
hypotheses.intervention: Leverage the intrinsic differences by operating under elevated temperature conditions to promote differential oxide growth; no compositional modification is introduced but the condition (temperature) is tuned to exaggerate oxide layer heterogeneity.
hypotheses.conditions: Simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (>300°C) where oxidation is accelerated and mechanical wear can selectively remove less-protective oxide regions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The heterogeneous passive films formed at the DR–IR interfaces, where the differences in oxide composition and thickness create localized sites of weakness.
hypotheses.mechanism: Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation and promotes the formation of passive films that differ in composition and adhesion on the dendritic versus interdendritic areas. Mechanical wear then preferentially removes the thinner or less adherent oxide in one region, exposing underlying phases with differing electrochemical potentials. This leads to strong galvanic coupling at the phase boundaries where the oxide is disrupted, thereby locally accelerating corrosion that feeds back into increased wear. The synergy between nonuniform oxide formation and selective film removal under wear conditions leads to accelerated coupled degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline tested at a lower temperature (with more uniform oxide films), the HEA under elevated temperature is expected to show a significant increase in total degradation. Specifically, higher corrosion current density and increased wear damage (deeper and wider wear tracks) are predicted, though the precise magnitude depends on the degree of oxide heterogeneity.
hypotheses.baseline: The same eutectic HEA operating under conditions where the oxide film forms more uniformly (e.g., lower temperature or under static conditions), resulting in a more homogeneous passive layer that better resists wear-corrosion coupling.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant when temperature is high enough to drive significantly different oxidation kinetics in the two regions and when wear stress can externally remove the weaker oxide portions; under isothermal or low-stress conditions the effect may be reduced.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact relative contributions of differential oxide formation and mechanical wear in driving galvanic coupling are not yet well quantified, making precise predictions of degradation rates uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the multi-phase eutectic HEA and expose them to high-temperature (e.g., 350°C) simultaneous wear–corrosion tests versus a matched set at a lower temperature. Use surface imaging (SEM/EDS) to map oxide film uniformity across dendritic vs interdendritic regions and conduct localized electrochemical measurements along with wear track profilometry.
measurements: Mapping of oxide film thickness and composition across DR and IR regions.
Electrochemical tests (icorr, EIS) taken from micro-regions.
Wear track characterization (depth and morphology).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If elevated temperature does not induce significant oxide layer heterogeneity at the DR–IR interfaces, or if the increased heterogeneity does not correlate with a measurable increase in galvanic corrosion and wear damage compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the understanding from the paper that different microstructural regions play distinct roles in wear and corrosion, combined with general principles of high-temperature oxidation and galvanic coupling from corrosion science.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely integrates the effect of differential oxide growth at inherent microstructural interfaces (dendritic vs interdendritic) and shows how their interaction under elevated temperatures accelerates degradation through localized galvanic effects—a mechanistic detail not previously considered in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Oxidation‐Induced Phase Transformation in Interdendritic Regions Triggers Localized Softening and Accelerated Wear–Corrosion.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA comprising a dendritic region enriched in certain elements and an interdendritic region containing Mo-rich σ phases and other intermetallics.
hypotheses.intervention: Exploit the operating condition by subjecting the HEA to elevated temperatures that drive oxidation-induced phase transformation specifically in the interdendritic regions without altering the initial composition.
hypotheses.conditions: Operating under simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (>300°C) where oxidation kinetics are high and can induce phase transformation or degradation of the interdendritic σ phase.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The integrity and phase composition of the interdendritic regions; specifically, the oxidation-induced transformation of Mo-rich σ phases into less protective, porous oxides.
hypotheses.mechanism: At high temperatures, the interdendritic regions experience rapid oxidation which drives partial transformation of stable Mo-rich σ phases into more porous, less adherent oxide products. This phase transformation softens the interdendritic areas, making them more susceptible to mechanical wear. Concurrently, the newly formed porous oxides are less effective as protective barriers, leading to further corrosion. The mutual reinforcement of these processes—wear exposing fresh material that oxidizes even more rapidly, and corrosion weakening the structure against wear—results in an accelerated overall degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy (or the same alloy operated at lower temperature) that maintains its original phase stability, the sample experiencing oxidation-induced phase transformation in the interdendritic regions is expected to show an increased wear rate (deeper, broader wear tracks) and higher corrosion current density. The overall degradation should accelerate appreciably, although the quantitative change remains to be experimentally determined.
hypotheses.baseline: A multi-phase eutectic HEA whose phase composition remains largely stable (with minimal oxidation-induced transformation) under less aggressive (lower temperature) or static conditions, leading to a more robust passive film and lower degradation rates.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism becomes dominant when operating temperatures are high enough to trigger oxidation-induced phase transformations and where cyclic wear continuously exposes the transformed, weakened areas; under isothermal or rapid passivation conditions the effect may diminish.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The extent to which the interdendritic σ phase transforms and how this affects local mechanical properties is not fully quantified, so the magnitude of degradation rate increase is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HEA samples and subject them to elevated temperature wear–corrosion tests while using XRD and microstructural imaging (SEM/TEM) to monitor any phase transformation in the interdendritic regions. Compare these with control samples tested under lower temperature or static conditions.
measurements: Phase analysis pre- and post-test (XRD, microscopy) to detect any oxidation‐induced transformation in interdendritic areas.
Quantitative wear track assessment (depth, width, and morphology).
Electrochemical measurements (icorr, impedance) to assess corrosion performance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no observable oxidation-induced phase transformation in the interdendritic regions or if the transformed regions do not correlate with increased wear and corrosion degradation compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

paper_did: Fabricated AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx high‐entropy alloy coatings on Q235 steel substrates via laser cladding with varied boron additions (x = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5).

Characterized the coatings’ microstructure using XRD, SEM, and EDS to reveal the retention of BCC and σ phases, the in situ formation of TiB2 particles, and the dendritic–interdendritic (DR–IR) segregation.

Conducted mechanical and electrochemical tests—including microhardness measurements, wear tests (friction coefficient, wear rate, and wear morphology) and corrosion evaluations (potentiodynamic polarization and EIS in 3.5 wt.% NaCl)—to correlate microstructural features with wear and corrosion resistance.
paper_reported: Boron addition induces the in situ formation of TiB2 particles whose size and volume fraction increase with B content, leading to significant lattice distortion and refinement of the BCC phase.

Enhanced microhardness and improved wear resistance (best performance at x = 1) were achieved via a combination of fine TiB2 dispersion, solid solution, and grain refinement effects, while excessive B (e.g., x = 1.5) promoted TiB2 agglomeration that spalls and degrades performance.

Corrosion tests showed that trace B additions improve passive film stability and reduce corrosion current density (icorr), whereas excessive B leads to passive film defects that accelerate pitting and galvanic corrosion.
paper_proposed: Future work is suggested to further optimize the coating through compositional tuning and post‐processing, and to explore performance aspects such as long‐term stability, machinability, and behavior under specific service environments.

expert_context.question: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of a HEA is governed by a load-induced tribocatalytic reaction that, in the presence of trace carbon-containing species, rapidly forms an amorphous carbon (a-C) tribolayer. This layer acts simultaneously as a solid lubricant (reducing wear) and a physical barrier (reducing corrosive attack).
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a nanostructured, 2D flake or layered morphology similar to (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2, deposited on stainless steel.
hypotheses.intervention: Utilize a controlled environment where the only variable is the availability of residual carbon species (e.g., from ethanol vs. an inert solvent such as distilled water) during sliding under corrosive conditions.
hypotheses.conditions: Perform ball-on-disk tests under identical loads and corrosive ambient (e.g., humid, oxygenated conditions) with the HEA lubricant applied using ethanol (carbon source) versus water (minimal carbon source).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: In situ generated a-C tribolayer at the sliding interface, integrated with retained HEA nanoflakes.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under high contact pressures, local flash temperatures and stress trigger tribocatalysis on the heterogeneous HEA surface. In the presence of ethanol, residual molecules decompose to form a lubricious amorphous carbon film that seals microcracks and physically isolates the underlying metal from the environment, thereby reducing both wear and corrosion. Without the carbon source, the protective film cannot form, exposing the substrate to higher degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The ethanol-based lubricant will show significantly lower total degradation (both lower wear rates in the 10^(-9) mm^3/N∙m range and reduced corrosion damage) relative to the water-based control; the beneficial effect should be evident under high loads. The effect is expected to diminish in environments devoid of carbon sources.
hypotheses.baseline: HEA tested with water-based lubrication and pure ethanol spray without HEA, where neither a protective tribofilm forms nor robust wear or corrosion mitigation is observed.
hypotheses.boundary: This prediction holds when the residual carbon source is present and the contact conditions promote sufficient tribocatalytic activity. It may fail if the ambient lacks carbon-containing species or if the sliding speeds/loads are too low to induce the necessary flash temperatures.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The quantitative impact on corrosion rates is not precisely predictable from current evidence, though the trend should be clear.

falsification_experiment.design: Run parallel tribo-corrosion tests using the same HEA coating under two conditions: one with ethanol as the solvent and one with water, while monitoring film formation and degradation rates over time.
measurements: Wear rate (mm^3/N∙m) via optical profilometry
Corrosion rate via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
Surface chemical analysis (Raman, TEM/EELS) to detect a-C tribolayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in wear and corrosion is observed between ethanol- and water-based tests, or if the a-C tribolayer is not detectable in the ethanol case, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s finding of tribocatalytic formation of a-C from ethanol on HEA nanoflakes under high load conditions.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It extends that mechanism to explain coupled wear–corrosion response by showing that the a-C layer, under tribo-corrosion conditions, acts also as a corrosion barrier; and proposes a controlled comparison (ethanol vs. water) to isolate this effect.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The hybrid wear–corrosion behavior of HEAs under tribo-corrosive conditions is governed by localized load-induced deformation that activates in situ oxidation of minority elements to form a passivating, mixed-metal oxide layer, which concurrently reduces mechanical damage and corrosion.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A bulk or thin-film high-entropy alloy with multiple transition metals that have varying oxidation tendencies, exhibiting nanoscale heterogeneity.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply an external load under environments with controlled oxygen availability while comparing tests performed in air versus those in an inert (e.g., argon) atmosphere.
hypotheses.conditions: Ball-on-disk experiment under high contact pressures in an environment with a controlled partial pressure of oxygen, alongside matched tests in an inert atmosphere, ensuring similar temperature and humidity.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A nanometer-thick, mixed-metal oxide film formed in situ at surface asperities where plastic deformation occurs.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under high stress, the HEA surface deforms and exposes reactive sites. In the presence of oxygen, minority elements (which may have higher oxidation tendencies) oxidize locally to form a thin, adherent, passivating oxide layer. This oxide film limits further oxidation and corrosion, while its ductile nature due to being ‘pre-strained’ by wear reduces friction and wear rates. Without oxygen, the lack of a protective oxide leads to higher wear and potential degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: In air (oxygen-rich), there will be lower observed total degradation with lower wear rates and improved corrosion resistance compared to tests performed in an inert environment. The oxide layer should be detectable by surface spectroscopy and microscopy, and its formation should correlate with reduced corrosion indicators.
hypotheses.baseline: Similar HEA under inert atmosphere (argon environment) where the passivating oxide film does not form, resulting in higher mechanical wear and unmitigated corrosion under tribological load.
hypotheses.boundary: This prediction holds when oxygen is available at sufficient levels to form the oxide layer and when the elemental composition supports selective oxidation. It may fail if the alloy composition is such that oxidation is too rapid or if the oxide layer is non-protective due to poor adherence.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact quantification of wear and corrosion reduction is uncertain because the oxidation kinetics might vary with microstructural details.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform tribo-corrosion tests on the HEA in both oxygen-rich (air) and oxygen-poor (argon) environments under identical mechanical loads, and analyze the surfaces for oxide films using XPS or Raman spectroscopy.
measurements: Wear rate and friction coefficient
Electrochemical corrosion rate
Surface oxide layer composition and thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-rich test does not produce an identifiable passivating oxide layer or does not show lower corrosion and wear compared to the inert condition, the hypothesis is refuted.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s mechanism of stress-induced transformations (though tribocatalysis with ethanol was emphasized) and background knowledge on passivation in corrosion (TXT::wikipedia::Corrosion::000).
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes that local deformation under load in HEAs may activate selective oxidation to form a passivating layer that simultaneously mitigates wear and corrosion, a mechanism not explored in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The simultaneous reduction in wear and corrosion in tribo-corrosion of HEAs is governed by the development of an adaptive dual-phase tribolayer that combines an amorphous carbon (a-C) component and an in situ precipitated, corrosion-resistant intermetallic phase. This dual-phase layer decreases mechanical degradation and limits corrosive pathways.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with nanoflake morphology and heterogeneous elemental distribution, similar to (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2, potentially modified with a small addition of a corrosion-resistant element (e.g., Cr or Al) to promote intermetallic formation.
hypotheses.intervention: Synthesize two HEA variants: one with the base composition and another with a minor alloying addition aimed at enhancing the formation of corrosion-resistant intermetallic precipitates during high shear, under tribo-corrosion conditions.
hypotheses.conditions: Conduct controlled ball-on-disk experiments in a corrosive environment (e.g., humid air with mild electrolytes) using an ethanol-based spray to supply carbon, and compare the dual-phase formation behavior in both compositions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: An in situ developed dual-phase tribolayer composed of an amorphous carbon film (from tribocatalytic reaction) and finely dispersed intermetallic precipitates that are inherently resistant to corrosion.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under high sliding loads in a corrosive environment, tribocatalytic reactions on the HEA surface produce an a-C film while, concurrently, localized plastic deformation and heterogeneous composition promote the precipitation of corrosion-resistant intermetallic phases. The synergy of the soft, lubricious carbon phase and the hard, protective intermetallics increases the contact area (reducing wear) and forms an effective barrier to corrosive species. Enhanced intermetallic formation in the modified HEA should further improve degradation resistance.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the base HEA, the modified alloy should exhibit lower total degradation, with both reduced wear rates (in the 10^(-9) mm^3/N∙m range) and enhanced corrosion resistance, attributable to a thicker and more robust dual-phase tribolayer. The coating might show a measurable increase in corrosion potential and reduced pit formation.
hypotheses.baseline: Base HEA composition under identical tribo-corrosion conditions where only an a-C tribolayer forms, leading to moderate protection against wear and corrosion.
hypotheses.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold when the additional element promotes controlled intermetallic precipitation without adversely affecting the intrinsic mechanical properties. It may fail if the added element disrupts the HEA’s phase stability or if the intermetallics are too brittle.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the qualitative dual-phase mechanism is supported, the precise proportional improvement in degradation resistance is uncertain due to complex interactions during tribolayer formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples (base and modified). Subject both to identical tribo-corrosion testing in an ethanol-containing corrosive environment, then characterize the tribolayer via TEM, EDS mapping, and corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization).
measurements: Wear rate measurements
Electrochemical corrosion metrics
Tribolayer composition and phase identification
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified HEA does not show a dual-phase tribolayer with improved wear and corrosion resistance compared to the base alloy, or if the intermetallic precipitation is absent or detrimental, the hypothesis is refuted.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation of an a-C tribolayer (PMC12019924::web::014) combined with general principles of phase evolution in HEAs (KG::phase_diagram::c5233d49ca).
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces a dual-phase tribolayer mechanism combining tribocatalytic a-C formation with stress-assisted intermetallic precipitation to explain coupled tribo-corrosion resistance, and proposes a compositional modification to test this effect.

paper_did: Synthesized a 2D high‐entropy alloy (HEA) (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 using chemical vapor transport followed by liquid‐phase exfoliation and spray coating on 304L stainless steel.
Conducted ball‐on‐disk tribological experiments under varying loads (1–9 N) in ambient conditions (25–40% RH, 20–25°C) to assess friction and wear performance.
Characterized the deposited coating and wear tracks using TEM, HAADF-STEM, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM, and EELS to determine structure and composition.
Demonstrated that under high contact pressures, a tribocatalytic reaction occurs whereby residual ethanol is decomposed into an amorphous carbon (a-C) tribofilm coexisting with HEA nanoflakes.
Performed MD simulations (ab initio and classical) to elucidate the two-step (dehydration and dehydrogenation) mechanism of ethanol decomposition on HEA surfaces.
Compared performance using ethanol-based versus water-based solvents, with ethanol enabling formation of the protective a-C layer and promoting low friction and wear rates.
paper_reported: Obtained unprecedented low coefficients of friction (down to ~0.076) and wear rates (~2.6×10⁻⁹ mm³ (N∙m)⁻¹) at high load, attributed to the unique tribological behavior of the 2D HEA.
Identified the formation of a tribofilm composed of HEA nanoflakes and an amorphous carbon layer through in situ tribocatalytic reactions during sliding.
Showed that the tribocatalytic reaction, confirmed by Raman and TEM/EELS data as well as MD simulations, converts ethanol to a-C, which under high load contributes to self-lubrication.
Demonstrated enhanced durability and extended wear life of the HEA coating, especially under high contact pressures, compared to conventional 2D lubricants.
Analyzed the mechanical properties (via elastic constant measurements) to show that the inherent deformability of the HEA aids in stress distribution and friction reduction.
paper_proposed: Development of a new class of advanced solid lubricants based on 2D HEAs leveraging their high compositional flexibility and low-shear-strength layered structure.
Utilization of simple spray coating techniques for application on complex geometries, potentially leading to cost-effective, oil-free tribological systems.
Further exploration of the tribocatalytic mechanism to optimize the formation of self-sustaining tribofilms for improved wear resistance.

testable.reason: The hypothesis offers a clear experimental design by comparing ethanol-based (carbon source) versus water-based lubrication under identical load and corrosive conditions with measurable wear and corrosion metrics.

beyond_paper.reason: It extends the paper’s findings by hypothesizing an additional corrosion barrier function of the a-C tribolayer, an aspect not addressed in the original study.

critique.fix: Enhance the hypothesis by providing preliminary evidence or literature support that stress-induced intermetallic precipitation is feasible in this HEA system, and clearly distinguish how this dual-phase formation could synergistically improve tribo-corrosion resistance.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: An in situ formed amorphous carbon (a-C) tribolayer that overlays the HEA surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under high contact pressures, friction-induced flash heating on the HEA initiates catalytic conversion of residual ethanol into an a-C film. This a-C layer, being chemically inert and continuous, acts as a physical barrier to both mechanical wear and corrosive species, thereby mitigating degradation. Its dual role is to smooth the sliding interface (reducing wear) and to limit the electrochemical access of corrosive agents to the metal surface (reducing corrosion).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The ethanol-based tests will exhibit a wear rate in the order of 10⁻⁹ mm³/(N·m) and lower corrosion current densities (as measured by electrochemical methods) relative to tests with a carbon-free solvent. Also, surface analysis will detect a continuous a-C layer only in the ethanol case.
hypotheses.baseline: HEA tested with a lubricant prepared using an inert, carbon-free solvent and a control test with pure ethanol without HEA, both of which do not form the protective a-C tribolayer.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective when frictional flash heating is sufficient to catalyze ethanol decomposition. It would fail in environments that are too cold or where the solvent lacks carbon species.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in corrosion current is not precisely predicted by available data.

hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between grain size reduction and corrosion passivation is not fully known.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Dynamic oxide regeneration governs the coupled tribo-corrosion response because wear continuously removes the passivating oxide layer, which then rapidly reforms from the high configurational entropy alloy constituents, creating a self-healing protective barrier.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) with an equiatomic mix similar to FeCoNiMnCu, possessing a thin thermally grown protective oxide layer formed under static high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject the HEA to controlled cyclical wear in a corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) while monitoring in situ oxide layer evolution, with one set having a pre-grown oxide and另一 set where the oxide is periodically removed.
hypotheses.conditions: Tests performed at ambient to moderately elevated temperature, in aqueous electrolyte, with wear generated by pin-on-disc at fixed load and sliding speed.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation and regeneration of mixed oxide phases (e.g., high-entropy spinel oxides and Cr2O3) at the worn surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: Wear mechanically disrupts the protective oxide film; however, due to the high entropy and element mobility in these alloys, a rapid re-oxidation occurs that reforms a barrier oxide. This dynamic balance between mechanical removal and oxidative healing governs the overall tribo-corrosion performance.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline HEA with a stable static oxide, samples subjected to cyclical wear would show lower total degradation because the reformed oxide protects the substrate. Both the wear and corrosion rates should be reduced by a moderate amount (the magnitude is uncertain without further calibration but expected to be in the tens of percent range) compared to conditions where no dynamic oxide regeneration is possible.
hypotheses.baseline: HEA samples with as-formed, non-regenerating oxide layers under static exposure.
hypotheses.boundary: The prediction should hold at temperatures and environmental conditions where oxidation kinetics are sufficiently fast; it may fail in low-oxygen or low-temperature environments that hinder re-oxidation.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative rates of oxide regeneration versus removal and the precise amounts of degradation reduction are uncertain.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The coupling of wear and corrosion in HEAs is governed by a balance between wear-induced microcrack formation and self-healing via high diffusion rates of alloying elements, resulting in transient localized corrosion followed by repassivation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An HEA with a uniform, equiatomic microstructure and an initially intact oxide layer formed during processing.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce controlled mechanical strain via repeated wear cycles that induce microcracks in the oxide and substrate. In parallel, modify the samples by a slight pre-annealing treatment to either enhance or suppress elemental diffusivity.
hypotheses.conditions: Tribological testing under cyclic loading in a corrosive medium (3.5 wt% NaCl), with a comparison between samples with enhanced diffusion (fast self-healing) and samples with reduced diffusion (via controlled heat treatment to encourage precipitate pinning).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Wear-induced microcracks and subsequent re-passivation zones where local diffusion of elements re-establishes protective oxides.
hypotheses.mechanism: Mechanical wear creates microcracks that expose fresh metal to the corrosive environment, leading to localized pits and accelerated anodic dissolution. However, due to the high diffusivity inherent to HEAs, especially when not kinetically impeded, atoms migrate to the damaged areas and reform protective oxide films that re-passivate the surface. The overall degradation is thus governed by the interplay between crack formation (accelerating corrosion) and diffusion-driven self-healing (inhibiting corrosion).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples with enhanced diffusivity (faster self-healing) will exhibit lower coupled degradation (both lower wear depth and reduced corrosion pit density) compared to the baseline. Conversely, samples with suppressed diffusion will show increased localized corrosion. The expected difference in degradation rates could be modest (~10-30%) but is mechanistically significant.
hypotheses.baseline: HEA samples in their as-processed state with standard diffusion rates and without induced microcrack management.
hypotheses.boundary: This prediction holds under conditions where temperature and alloy composition permit significant atomic mobility; it would fail at very low temperatures where diffusion is negligible.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise diffusion rates and the quantitative balance of crack formation versus healing are not well-established in the literature.

hypotheses.uncertainty: The details of the phase transformation kinetics and the exact identity of the precipitated phases in the tribo-corrosion context remain uncertain.

In contrast, samples that do not form this deformation-induced layer will show higher coupled degradation.

The improvement is expected to be moderate (perhaps 10–30% lower degradation), though the precise quantitative improvement is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: HEA samples with as-deposited, coarser microstructures from microwave cladding, without additional strain-induced nanocrystallization.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to be effective when the applied deformation is sufficient to induce nanocrystallization without causing excessive microcracking; it may fail if the wear conditions are too mild (insufficient strain) or too severe (inducing detrimental cracking).
hypotheses.uncertainty: The balance between beneficial hardening due to nanocrystallization and potential adverse effects from microcrack formation is not fully characterized, and the quantitative reduction in degradation remains approximate.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The tribo-corrosion response of the HEA is governed by the dynamic stability of its passive oxide film, where mechanical wear intermittently disrupts the protective film and the re-passivation kinetics dictate the coupled degradation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA with its inherent multiphase microstructure and naturally formed passive film in corrosive environments.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a controlled post-casting heat treatment aimed at optimizing the oxide scale formation (e.g., a short-term oxidation heat treatment in air) to generate a more uniform and adherent passive film.
hypotheses.conditions: Testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl under cyclic tribological loading (mimicking tribo-corrosion conditions) in a controlled laboratory setup.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A modified and more chemically bonded oxide film covering a more homogenized microstructure.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the mechanical removal of the passive film exposes fresh material; if the re-passivation kinetics are slow, the corrosion component is enhanced due to localized attack (as observed by potential shifts and EN analysis in the paper). Enhancing film formation via heat treatment should lead to a resilient passive layer that is less prone to mechanical disruption, thereby reducing the cycle of damage and repassivation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The heat-treated HEA will show lower total mass loss compared to the untreated baseline, with a decrease in corrosion-driven degradation while the wear component might be similar. The improved re-passivation should result in a measurable reduction in corrosion current (Icorr) and more stable open-circuit potential curves under cyclic loading.
hypotheses.baseline: The original as-cast, untreated CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA under identical tribo-corrosion testing conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: The prediction holds if the failure mode is mostly driven by passive film disruption rather than by bulk mechanical damage. It might fail in regimes where excessive mechanical loading completely removes the oxide regardless of its adhesion.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise degree of improvement in re-passivation kinetics and its quantitative effect on mass loss under tribo-corrosion is uncertain.

hypotheses.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by reducing the Cu content to suppress the formation of Cu-rich segregations, thereby producing a more homogeneous microstructure with diminished galvanic couples.
hypotheses.conditions: Tribological testing in the same 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, under cyclic mechanical loading that replicates the tribo-corrosion environment, with both the modified alloy and the original serving as direct comparisons.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A more uniform microstructure with minimized intermetallic segregation and less pronounced compositional gradients at phase boundaries.
hypotheses.mechanism: Localized corrosion is enhanced at phase boundaries where compositional disparities (e.g., Cu-rich vs. matrix) establish micro-galvanic cells. Under mechanical loading, these regions experience accelerated damage due to reduced cohesive strength and selective phase removal. By reducing Cu, the driving force for selective phase corrosion is lowered, which in turn should mitigate the synergistic interaction between mechanical wear and localized corrosion.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA with lower Cu content should exhibit reduced localized corrosion marks (verified by fewer micro-cracks and less mass loss localized at phase boundaries) and overall lower tribo-corrosion degradation compared to the baseline alloy. The total degradation rate, particularly the corrosion component, is expected to decrease.

hypotheses.boundary: This prediction holds in corrosive environments where galvanic interactions due to microstructural heterogeneity are the dominant mechanism. It may fail if homogeneous wear mechanisms predominate or if Cu reduction adversely affects other protective attributes of the HEA.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The quantitative balance between reduced galvanic corrosion and possible impacts on mechanical properties due to Cu reduction is uncertain.

hypotheses.material_initial_state: An as-cast high-entropy alloy in its original state where repetitive tribological impacts induce work hardening and associated changes in hardness (observed increase from ~567 to over 930 HV after prolonged CE in the paper).

paper_did: Synthesized as‐cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA via an arc melting process using high‐purity raw metals.
Conducted cavitation erosion tests in both 3.5 wt% NaCl solution and deionized water under ASTM G32-10 conditions (20 kHz, 2.5 kW, 60 μm amplitude).

Performed electrochemical measurements including potentiodynamic polarization, open-circuit potential (OCP) monitoring (with cyclic CE/quiescence), and electrochemical noise (EN) analysis (with wavelet processing).
Characterized the microstructure and phase distribution using XRD, EBSD, and SEM-EDS, and evaluated surface damage, roughness, and hardness evolution after varying CE times.
Quantitatively analyzed the synergistic effects of corrosion and CE and identified damage progression from FCC phase exfoliation to degradation of intermetallic σ and μ phases.
paper_reported: The cumulative mass loss increased with CE time and was higher in 3.5 wt% NaCl than in deionized water, with a significant contribution (48.02%) from the synergistic effect between corrosion and CE.

The damage mechanism evolved from the selective exfoliation of the softer FCC phase to further degradation of the harder intermetallic σ and μ phases, as evidenced by microstructure and surface roughness analyses.

Electrochemical testing revealed that cavitation conditions significantly accelerated the cathodic reaction (evidenced by an upward shift in Ecorr and an increase in Icorr) due to enhanced oxygen transport, while OCP cycles reflected the competing effects of passive film breakup and re-passivation.
Wavelet and EN analyses indicated that with extended CE, the nature of corrosion shifted from localized selective phase corrosion to a regime dominated by passive film dynamics.
paper_proposed: Although not explicitly outlined in a dedicated future work section, the study implies that a deeper understanding of the interplay between mechanical damage (CE) and corrosion—especially the roles of passive film formation, selective phase attack, and work-hardening behavior—is key to guiding the design of HEAs with improved CE-corrosion resistance in marine environments.

hypotheses.hypothesis: In a tribo-corrosion environment, the coupling between wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the stability and self-healing of the passive film, which is enhanced by the presence of finely dispersed in situ TiB2 particles. These particles act as nucleation sites for passive film repair and mitigate localized galvanic cells by reducing cathodic area differences during mechanical wear.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A base AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy prepared via laser cladding, initially featuring a dual-phase BCC + σ structure without excessive coarse ceramic particles.
hypotheses.intervention: Control the boron addition and laser cladding parameters to produce a uniform dispersion of fine TiB2 reinforcements rather than clustered or oversized particles.
hypotheses.conditions: Experiments conducted in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under sliding wear conditions (20 N load, similar to the original study parameters) to simulate tribo-corrosion.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed fine TiB2 particles distributed within the alloy matrix and at phase boundaries.
hypotheses.mechanism: The fine TiB2 particles promote grain refinement and provide active sites for rapid passive film regeneration when the film is mechanically disrupted by wear. They also reduce galvanic coupling by limiting the size and continuity of cathodic sites (e.g., large TiB2 clusters), thereby simultaneously reducing the wear rate and the corrosion current density.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline with either no or excessive boron addition, the optimized dispersion is expected to reduce the total degradation by lowering wear rate (potentially by ~50% relative improvement over a coarse-particle sample) and decreasing corrosion current density (icorr reduction similar to or improved upon the 51% reduction seen with small boron addition).
hypotheses.baseline: The baseline is the same HEA coating without controlled fine TiB2 distribution (either B-free or with coarse/agglomerated TiB2 particles).
hypotheses.boundary: The prediction should hold in environments where mechanical wear intermittently disrupts the passive film, such as in mild to moderate tribo-corrosion conditions. It may fail if the tribological load is so high that even rapid film regeneration cannot compensate for film removal, or if the environmental corrosivity overwhelms the passive film healing.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in wear and corrosion metrics is uncertain beyond qualitative trends, and scale-up effects during extended cycling are not quantified.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The mechanical degradation under tribo-corrosion in high-entropy alloys is predominantly governed by grain boundary density, where a finer grain structure facilitates quicker re-passivation of exposed surfaces. hypotheses.structural_mediator: An increased density of grain boundaries within a refined microstructure.

Simultaneously, the refined structure increases hardness (via the Hall–Petch effect), reducing wear depth.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Minor yttrium addition enhances the adhesion and integrity of the passivating composite oxide layer, reducing its spallation under combined mechanical and corrosive stress.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A strongly amorphous AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) film produced by Co-FCVAD, as reported in the paper, which forms a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer upon annealing at high temperature.
hypotheses.intervention: Incorporate 1–2 at.% Y into the HEA composition during deposition.
hypotheses.conditions: Subject the Y-modified HEA film to the same thermal shock (annealing at 800 °C for 1 h in air) and tribo-corrosion testing (reciprocating wear in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) as the baseline.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation of a Y-enriched oxide interface that enhances the bonding between the oxide layer and the underlying HEA substrate.
hypotheses.mechanism: Yttrium is known to improve oxide adhesion (as seen in superalloys where yttrium additions promote oxide layer adherence and reduce spallation [TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::020]). By forming a Y-rich interfacial phase, the oxide film becomes more resistant to mechanical removal during wear, sustaining its protective barrier function against both mechanical and electrochemical degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Total degradation will be reduced, with lower wear rates and smaller potential fluctuations (e.g., lower ΔOCP) compared to the baseline AlCrTiZrMo film without Y. The oxide film is expected to exhibit enhanced continuity and resistance to mechanical disruption.
hypotheses.baseline: The original AlCrTiZrMo film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h that produces a dense ZrTiO4 oxide layer but shows limitations in oxide spallation under severe tribological conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: This prediction should hold in environments where oxide spallation is the primary pathway for degradation. In extremely aggressive dynamic loading that mechanically disrupts any oxide layer regardless of adhesion, the beneficial effect might be diminished.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While literature supports improved adhesion via rare earth additions in other alloy systems, the exact extent of improvement in tribo-corrosion resistance in this specific HEA under the test conditions may vary and needs quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA films: one with the 1–2 at.% Y addition and one without (control). Anneal both at 800 °C for 1 h and conduct identical tribo-corrosion tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution using a reciprocating tribometer with real-time OCP and COF monitoring.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³·N⁻¹·m⁻¹)
ΔOCP during loading
Coefficient of friction
Surface oxide morphology and adherence (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-modified film does not exhibit statistically lower wear rate, smaller ΔOCP, and improved oxide adherence compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.what_is_new: The intervention of adding yttrium to enhance oxide layer adhesion has not been reported in the paper and provides a novel approach to mitigate coupled tribo-corrosion by specifically targeting oxide spallation.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A compressively stressed surface state can enhance the integrity and resilience of the passivating oxide layer, thereby mitigating the synergistic effects of wear and corrosion.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: The amorphous AlCrTiZrMo HEA film that, after high temperature annealing at 800 °C, forms a dense oxide layer but is still vulnerable to microcrack initiation and spallation under cyclic mechanical loading.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a controlled mechanical pre-deformation (e.g., shot peening) to induce a compressive residual stress state in the near-surface region prior to annealing.
hypotheses.conditions: Apply the pre-deformation on the as-deposited HEA film, then anneal at 800 °C for 1 h in air, and finally subject it to identical tribo-corrosion testing (reciprocating sliding in corrosive electrolyte) as the non-deformed baseline.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The compressive residual stress field in the near-surface region that reduces microcracking and delamination of the passivating oxide layer.
hypotheses.mechanism: Compressive stresses are well known to inhibit crack initiation and propagation. By imparting a compressive state before thermal treatment, the oxide layer that subsequently forms may be under less tensile stress during wear. This reduces the formation of microcracks that serve as sites for corrosive attack, thereby lowering both wear and corrosion concurrently. Similar compressive strategies are used in superalloys and thermal barrier coatings to enhance oxidation resistance [TXT::wikipedia::Thermal_barrier_coating::004].
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A reduced overall degradation is expected, with improved tribocorrosion resistance (i.e., lower wear rates, smaller fluctuations in OCP) relative to the untreated baseline. The oxide layer should show fewer microcracks and superior adhesion.
hypotheses.baseline: The HEA film processed without pre-deformation but annealed under the same conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism should be effective under conditions where mechanical cycling-induced tensile stresses are a primary cause of oxide disruption. Its effectiveness may diminish if the pre-deformation induces detrimental plastic flow or if the film's amorphous structure negates the benefits of residual stress.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The magnitude and distribution of the beneficial compressive stress may vary with the pre-deformation parameters, and the optimum processing window is not precisely known.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observation that a stable dense oxide layer improves tribocorrosion performance by maintaining integrity under load, extending it by enhancing the oxide's mechanical resilience via residual stress engineering.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes the use of mechanical pre-deformation (shot peening) to introduce beneficial compressive stresses, a strategy not reported in the paper for tuning the coupled tribo-corrosion response of HEA films.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Nanocrystalline carbide dispersoids within the amorphous matrix act as diffusion barriers, limiting oxygen ingress along internal boundaries, and therefore modulate both the mechanical wear and corrosion processes under tribo-corrosion conditions.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: The as-deposited amorphous AlCrTiZrMo HEA film which, upon annealing (800 °C for 1 h), forms a dense oxide layer but may have grain boundaries or residual regions that allow oxygen diffusion during wear.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a trace addition (∼1 at.%) of Nb during deposition to promote the in-situ formation of nanocrystalline NbC (or similar carbide) dispersoids uniformly distributed in the amorphous matrix.
hypotheses.conditions: Deposit the Nb-doped HEA film using modified Co-FCVAD, anneal at 800 °C for 1 h in air, and then perform identical tribo-corrosion testing (reciprocating sliding in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) as for the baseline film.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale carbide precipitates that pin internal boundaries and reduce fast oxygen diffusion pathways, reinforcing the overall microstructural integrity during wear-corrosion coupling.
hypotheses.mechanism: Nanocrystalline carbides are known to act as barriers to diffusive processes. Their presence within the amorphous matrix would hinder the transport of oxygen along possible fast diffusion paths (e.g., at internal boundaries) and reduce localized oxidation at freshly exposed surfaces during wear. This, in turn, ensures that the passivating oxide layer remains more uniform and less likely to be undermined by rapid internal oxidation. This mechanism is analogous to dispersion strengthening and diffusion barrier strategies used in other alloy systems [KG::intermetallic::0646f6391c].
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The Nb-doped HEA film is predicted to exhibit lower overall degradation under tribo-corrosion. Specifically, it should have reduced localized corrosion (as evidenced by smaller OCP drops) and lower wear rates relative to the matched baseline without Nb.
hypotheses.baseline: The pure AlCrTiZrMo film without Nb additions, processed and tested under identical conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism should be effective in environments where oxygen transport is a limiting factor for corrosion, but might be less effective in regimes where mechanical abrasion is so severe that the diffusion barriers are mechanically destroyed.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The actual volume fraction and distribution of NbC dispersoids and their effect on oxygen diffusion kinetics remain to be quantitatively established, so precise improvements in tribo-corrosion resistance warrant experimental validation.

hypotheses.what_is_new: The use of a carbide-forming element (Nb) to create internal diffusion barriers is a new approach relative to the paper, offering an alternate route to enhancing tribo-corrosion resistance by modifying the material’s microstructural diffusion dynamics.

paper_did: Prepared strongly amorphous AlCrTiZrMo HEA films using co‐filter cathode vacuum arc deposition (Co‐FCVAD) on stainless steel and silicon substrates.
Executed high‐temperature annealing treatments at 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C for 1 h in air to study thermal‐shock and oxidation effects.
Characterized the films’ microstructure and composition with SEM, EDS, TEM, and XRD.
Measured changes in mechanical properties (hardness and Young’s modulus) after annealing.
Tested tribocorrosion performance by monitoring open circuit potential (OCP), coefficient of friction (COF), and wear rate during reciprocating sliding in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
paper_reported: The as-deposited film is strongly amorphous, which contributes to a slow oxygen diffusion rate.
Annealing at 800 °C leads to the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer that effectively halts further oxidation.

The film annealed at 800 °C exhibits enhanced mechanical properties (hardness up to 20.88 GPa and modulus up to 220.2 GPa) and the best tribocorrosion resistance (ΔOCP = 0.055, COF = 0.04, wear rate = 1.34 × 10⁻⁶ mm³·N⁻¹·m⁻¹).
paper_proposed: The work suggests that understanding and optimizing the protection mechanisms in HEA films—particularly the role of the dense oxide layer—can improve performance in extreme environments.
It hints at the need for further exploration of mechanism research, functional design, and process optimization of HEA films to enhance oxidation and tribocorrosion resistance.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Post-annealing cooling rate controls the formation of a graded, low‐stress oxide scale that governs the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An amorphous AlCrTiZrMo HEA film deposited by Co-FCVAD that, when annealed at 800 °C for 1 h, forms a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer.
hypotheses.intervention: After high-temperature annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, apply two different controlled cooling protocols: one with slow, furnace cooling and one with rapid quenching.
hypotheses.conditions: Both sets of samples are subjected to the same tribo-corrosion testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution using a reciprocating sliding setup.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A graded oxide scale featuring a gradual transition in microstructure and residual stress from the outer, hard ZrTiO4 layer to the underlying HEA substrate.
hypotheses.mechanism: Slow cooling minimizes thermal gradients and residual tensile stresses in the oxide, allowing the formation of a coherent graded oxide layer with fewer microcracks. This graded structure enhances both wear and corrosion resistance by reducing crack initiation (mechanically) and hindering oxygen diffusion (electrochemically). In contrast, rapid quenching can introduce high residual stresses and microcrack networks within the oxide, which would accelerate degradation under tribological and corrosive loading. (See also TXT::wikipedia::Thermal_barrier_coating::004 for the importance of matching thermal stresses.)
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples will exhibit lower overall degradation, with reduced wear rates and smaller fluctuations in OCP (ΔOCP) compared to quenched samples. The improvement is expected to be moderate—likely on the order of 15–30% lower degradation markers—if thermal shock does not override the graded oxide benefits.
hypotheses.baseline: The standard processing route with rapid cooling (or uncontrolled cooling) immediately after annealing at 800 °C.
hypotheses.boundary: This effect should hold in environments where thermal gradients during cooling can be controlled. In service conditions that impose very rapid cyclic thermal shocks or where cooling rates are dictated by external conditions, the benefits might be diminished.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement depends on the cooling rate achieved and the stress relaxation kinetics; detailed thermal analysis is required to optimize parameters.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and ΔOCP and do not show evidence of a graded, lower-stress oxide microstructure compared to the quenched samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the idea that post-annealing cooling rate can be deliberately modified to create a graded oxide layer with improved mechanical integrity and corrosion resistance—a processing parameter not explored in the paper.

paper_did: Prepared amorphous AlCrTiZrMo HEA films by Co-FCVAD on 304 stainless steel and silicon wafer substrates.
Applied high-temperature annealing at 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C for 1 h in an air environment to probe thermal shock effects.

Characterized the films’ microstructure (via SEM, TEM, XRD), elemental composition (EDS), mechanical properties (nanoindentation for hardness and Young’s modulus), and tribocorrosion performance (using reciprocating sliding tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution with monitoring of OCP, COF, and wear rate).
paper_reported: At 800 °C for 1 h, a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer forms on the film surface that effectively arrests further oxidation.

Mechanical properties are enhanced with higher annealing temperatures – with hardness and elastic modulus peaking at 20.88 GPa and 220.2 GPa, respectively – and tribocorrosion performance improves significantly (ΔOCP = 0.055, COF = 0.04, wear rate = 1.34×10⁻⁶ mm³·N⁻¹·m⁻¹) for the 800 °C annealed films.

The formation of the protective oxide scale and the concurrent microstructural densification of the amorphous film are identified as key mechanisms behind improved oxidation and tribocorrosion resistance.
paper_proposed: Investigating the protection mechanism of HEA films under extreme environments by studying the influence of thermal shock (annealing conditions) on oxide formation and microstructure.

Exploring process optimization strategies for HEA films – particularly regarding the balance between oxidation and mechanical integrity under thermal shock – though without altering the baseline cooling or composition.
